text:
**Yes, the AC180 is worth it at about $450-$475, as long as you mostly run AC appliances and don't need to carry it much.** At the $499 list price it's less of a bargain.

**What it does well**
- **Real capacity:** Six independent tests measured about 991 Wh usable out of the rated 1,152 Wh, roughly 82-90% ([Watt Power Station](https://wattpowerstation.com/power-stations/bluetti-ac180/)). PCWorld found its AC efficiency among the best it had tested ([PCWorld](https://www.pcworld.com/article/1966571/bluetti-ac180-power-station-review.html)).
- **Power and longevity:** It delivers 1,800 W continuous (2,700 W surge) from a LiFePO4 battery rated for 3,500+ cycles, with a 5-year warranty and 0-80% charging in about 45 minutes ([BLUETTI](https://www.bluettipower.com/products/ac180?variant=44099774480603)).
- **Value:** It has one of the lower costs per usable Wh among the models Watt Power Station tracks, at about $0.45/Wh ([Watt Power Station](https://wattpowerstation.com/power-stations/bluetti-ac180/)).

**Downsides**
- **Weight:** At about 36 lb it's heavy for its capacity. OutdoorGearLab scored it only 66/100 for this reason and for its noisy fan ([OutdoorGearLab](https://www.outdoorgearlab.com/reviews/camping-and-hiking/power-station/bluetti-ac180)).
- **Small loads:** It's inefficient on small DC loads. PCWorld measured 71% on a USB-PD-style load, and Outdoor Life got only 54% at a 34 W load, which matters for a CPAP or an overnight fridge ([iTechGuides](https://www.itechguides.com/bluetti-ac180-power-station-review-excellent-ac-efficiency-but-heavy-and-less-impressive-over-dc/), [Watt Power Station](https://wattpowerstation.com/power-stations/bluetti-ac180/)).
- **2,700 W mode:** The 2,700 W Power Lifting mode is only for resistive heating loads. Output also drops to 1,500 W in high heat ([Best Batteries](https://us.best-batteries.com/reviews/bluetti-ac180/)).
- **Expandability:** Sources disagree on this. Bluetti's page advertises expansion batteries, but Watt Power Station says Bluetti's own FAQ says it isn't expandable. Confirm with Bluetti before buying if you're counting on it.
- **Availability:** Best Batteries reports it discontinued in Europe, and iTechGuides saw mixed stock signals in the US, so check that your exact variant is in stock.

**Alternatives**
OutdoorGearLab recommends the successor, the BLUETTI Elite 100 V2. It's lighter (25 lb), quieter and charges faster, with a smaller 1,024 Wh battery. It lists around $489 ([OutdoorGearLab](https://www.outdoorgearlab.com/reviews/camping-and-hiking/power-station/bluetti-ac180), [Watt Power Station](https://wattpowerstation.com/power-stations/bluetti-ac180/)). The Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2 is about $499.99 with similar usable capacity. I don't have buy links for either from these results.

**Where to buy**
- **BLUETTI direct, $499:** [bluettipower.com AC180](https://www.bluettipower.com/products/ac180?variant=44099774480603). It includes a 30-day price-match guarantee and free shipping.
- **Amazon, about $449** as of Oct 24 per iTechGuides. Their page lists several AC180 variants, so verify which one you're getting ([iTechGuides](https://www.itechguides.com/bluetti-ac180-power-station-review-excellent-ac-efficiency-but-heavy-and-less-impressive-over-dc/)).
- **With code AFF5OFF, $474.05:** [Dealectric link](https://dealectric.com/go/bluetti-ac180). That's the Bluetti store, and Dealectric earns a commission. Its code was last tested Oct 21, so confirm it applies at checkout. Amazon's price may still beat it.

If you want to add solar, the AC180 + 200 W panel kit is $769 at BLUETTI, or $730.55 with the code ([Dealectric](https://dealectric.com/go/bluetti-ac180-200w-solar-kit)).

If you tell me what you'd power (fridge, CPAP, camping gear) and how often you'd move it, I can say whether this or a lighter unit fits better.
